# Bytes from foreign implementations

Run on 2026-08-09 on the Linux test host. Each row is one IDL type
filled with one fixed sample and handed to a vendor's own serialiser.
Nothing in this project produced any of these bytes.

**Serialiser, not socket.** Every entry point named below is in-memory.
Where a vendor's transport layer decides the same question differently,
these bytes are not what a peer sees, and two such questions are
measured: the encapsulation options field (`docs/wire-feature-inventory.md`
B5 — RTI's static plugin leaves it zero, its RTPS layer sets it) and the
content of alignment padding (`tools/wire-capture` — RTI, Fast DDS and
JacORB write zero on the wire; omniORB and TAO write the previous
message's octets, and the zeros recorded here for TAO are the probe's
fresh buffer). Every sentence below about padding content, about the
encapsulation header, or about what a vendor "writes on the wire" is a
sentence about the serialiser named in the table.

| | |
|---|---|
| Eclipse Cyclone DDS | `/opt/cyclone`, `idlc` + `dds_stream_write_sampleLE` |
| RTI Connext DDS | 7.7.0, `rtiddsgen -language C` + `<T>Plugin_serialize_to_cdr_buffer_ex` |
| eProsima Fast DDS | `fastddsgen` + Fast CDR `Cdr` in `XCDRv1` / `XCDRv2` |

Three constructs are outside what those three can be asked, and the last
section measures them somewhere else. Nothing there produced a byte this
project decided either.

| | |
|---|---|
| OpenDDS | 3.34.0, `opendds_idl` + `OpenDDS::DCPS::Serializer`. A fourth DDS implementation, and the only one whose IDL front end takes a `map`. |
| omniORB | 4.3.3, `omniidl -bcxx` + `cdrMemoryStream`. A CORBA ORB, for `fixed<P,S>`, which is a CORBA type no DDS generator carries. |
| JacORB | 3.9, `org.jacorb.idl.parser` + `CDROutputStream`. A second ORB, to separate the rule from one ORB's reading of it. |
| TAO | 2.5.24, `tao_idl -as` + `TAO_OutputCDR`. A third ORB, added when the ORBs stopped being a one-question oracle. |

The three ORBs were asked one question each until 2026-08-10. Since
then they are a column: XCDR1 *is* CORBA CDR — CORBA 3.3 part 2 §9.3 —
so an ORB is a reference for the whole shared base and not only for the
one type XTypes left out. **The CORBA column** below is that run;
`docs/corba-column.md` is its argument and its corpus totals.

The harness is [`tools/byte-gate/`](../../../../tools/byte-gate/): one
directory per case holding the IDL, the top-level type name, and the C
or C++ statements that fill the sample. `gate.sh --cases <name>`
generates, compiles and runs each vendor. It lived at
`/root/byte-gate/gate` on the test host until it was brought into the
repository; [`docs/interop-harnesses.md`](../../../../docs/interop-harnesses.md)
is the index of every harness that produced a figure in this project.

**Which of these rows a pipeline can regenerate** is in
[`vendor_bytes.rows.tsv`](vendor_bytes.rows.tsv) beside this file — the
machine-readable form of what the sections below narrate, one row per
(case, vendor, encoding, byte order). `tools/byte-gate/verify.sh`
regenerates it and fails on any row that differs, and the
`interop-vendor-bytes` job runs that on every merge request against
Cyclone, Fast DDS and OpenDDS in the pinned `ci-interop` image.

| vendor | recorded rows | of which bytes | regenerated by the pipeline |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Cyclone DDS | 272 | 196 | yes |
| Fast DDS | 272 | 188 | yes |
| OpenDDS | 272 | 16 | yes |
| RTI Connext | 272 | 188 | **no** — licensed and machine-bound, host only |

Every case is a row for every vendor. A vendor that produced no bytes
says why in the same eight columns: `ungenerated` where its front end
would not parse the type, `uncompiled` where the generated code would
not build, and `unfilled` where this harness has no sample in that
vendor's language mapping — the last being a statement about this
repository and not about the vendor. None of the three is a blank.
Every table
below that names one of the four vendors is regenerated for three of
them and re-derived on the test host for the fourth. The ORB rows of
**The CORBA column** and the `fixed<P,S>` rows are neither: their
toolchains are not in the image and `tools/corba-oracle/` and
`tools/wire-oracle/fixed-orbs.sh` produce them on the host.

Byte counts exclude the four-byte encapsulation header. Fast DDS's
header byte is not reported in the little-endian rows — the harness
calls `serialize_encapsulation()` itself before handing the sample to
the generated code, so the header reflects the harness, not the vendor.
The body does come from the generated `serialize`.

The big-endian section at the end does report it, for all three: it was
measured through `tools/wireprobe/`, whose Fast DDS probe runs the
generated `<T>PubSubType` and takes the encoding flag from the header
that writes.

## Where all three agree

These fix rules the planner must follow.

### Maximum alignment under XCDR2 is four

```idl
@final struct Point { long x; double y; };   // x = 1, y = 2.0
```

| | XCDR1 | XCDR2 |
|---|---|---|
| Cyclone | `01000000 00000000 00000000 00000040` (16) | `01000000 00000000 00000040` (12) |
| RTI | identical (16) | identical (12) |
| Fast DDS | identical (16) | identical (12) |

The double sits at offset 8 under XCDR1 and at offset 4 under XCDR2.

```idl
@final struct Mixed {
    boolean b; octet o; short s; unsigned short us;
    long l; unsigned long ul; long long ll; unsigned long long ull;
    float f; double d;
};
```

with `b=true, o=0xAB, s=-12345, us=54321, l=-1234567, ul=2345678,
ll=-987654321, ull=123456789, f=2.5, d=3.14159`:

| | bytes |
|---|---|
| XCDR1, all three | `01abc7cf31d40000 7929edff ceca2300 4f9721c5ffffffff 15cd5b0700000000 00002040 00000000 6e861bf0f9210940` (48) |
| XCDR2, all three | `01abc7cf31d40000 7929edff ceca2300 4f9721c5ffffffff 15cd5b0700000000 00002040 6e861bf0f9210940` (44) |

Only the four padding bytes before the trailing double differ.

This is the measurement that retired wire vector V-3. See
`Encoding::max_alignment` and the note above
`v3_final_mixed_primitives_plans_forty_four_under_xcdr2`.

### Everything else all three agree on

| case | IDL | XCDR1 | XCDR2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `array` | `long a[3]; double d[2];` | 32 | 28 |
| `enumeration` | `Colour c; long x;` | 8 | 8 |
| `keyed` | `@key long id; long x;` | 8 | 8 |
| `string_member` | `string s; long n;` with `s="abc"` | 12 | 12 |
| `seq_long` | `sequence<long> ids;` with 3 elements | 16 | 16 |
| `union_case` | `union switch(long) { case 1: long a; default: double b; }` | 8 | 8 |
| `ext_final` | `@final { long a; double b; short c; }` | 18 | 14 |
| `ext_appendable` | the same, `@appendable` | 18 | 18 (DHEADER `0e000000`) |
| `mut_optional` XCDR2 | `@mutable { long a; @optional long b; }`, `b` absent | — | `08000000 00000020 07000000` (12) |

`ext_appendable` under XCDR1 carries no delimiter: XCDR1 has no
delimited encoding, so `@appendable` and `@final` are the same bytes.

A `@mutable` type's absent `@optional` member is simply not written:
the parameter list is what says which members are there, so an absent
one leaves no trace. That is what `mut_optional` above records, and it
is **not** what happens outside a `@mutable` type — see the next
section.

### An `@optional` member of a type that is not `@mutable`

```idl
@final struct Sample { long a; @optional octet b; long c; };
```

`a = -1234567`, `b = 0xAB`, `c = -2`, little endian. Run 2026-08-09
through `tools/byte-gate/`, cases `opt_final_present` and
`opt_final_absent`.

| | XCDR2, present | XCDR2, absent |
|---|---|---|
| Cyclone | `7929edff 01 ab 0000 feffffff` (12) | `7929edff 00000000 feffffff` (12) |
| RTI | `7929edff 01 ab 0400 feffffff` (12) | `7929edff 00000000 feffffff` (12) |
| Fast DDS | `7929edff 01 ab 0100 feffffff` (12) | `7929edff 00000000 feffffff` (12) |

| | XCDR1, present | XCDR1, absent |
|---|---|---|
| Cyclone | `7929edff 017f0800 01000000 01000000 ab000000 feffffff` (24) | `7929edff 017f0800 01000000 00000000 feffffff` (20) |
| RTI | `7929edff 01000400 ab000000 feffffff` (16) | `7929edff 01000000 feffffff` (12) |
| Fast DDS | `7929edff 01000100 ab000000 feffffff` (16) | `7929edff 01000000 feffffff` (12) |

**All three write a marker, in both encoding versions, whether or not
the member has a value.** This is §7.4.3.5.2 rule (20) under XCDR2 — a
BOOLEAN `<is_present>`, then the value — and §7.4.1.2 under XCDR1: "If
the member takes no value within that particular object, the data
length indicated by the header shall be zero." The two bytes after `01`
in the XCDR2 present rows are padding before `c` and their content is
not fixed by any clause; RTI and Fast DDS leave whatever was there.

The XCDR1 rows also settle a question the `@mutable` measurement in §2
could not: **what the declared length counts depends on the parameter's
role, not only on the implementation.** Cyclone declares `1` for the
one-byte `@optional octet` here and `4` for the two-byte `short c` of
`ext_mutable`. RTI declares the padded length in both places, Fast DDS
the true length in both. `PlCdr1HeaderPolicy::pads_declared_length` and
`pads_declared_optional_length` are those two axes.

This project wrote an EMHEADER under XCDR2 and nothing at all for an
absent member under either version until this run. For
`@optional octet b` that is sixteen bytes against twelve with the value
at offset 8 against offset 5, and it could not be exchanged with any of
the three in either direction.

### A structure has no trailing padding

```idl
@final struct Odd { long a; short b; };
```

All three, both versions: `010000000200` — six bytes, not eight. The
type aligns to four but does not pad out to it.

### Array elements pad between themselves, not after the last

```idl
@final struct Odd { long a; short b; };
@final struct ArrOdd { Odd items[2]; octet tail; };
```

All three under XCDR1, and RTI under XCDR2:

```
01000000 0200 0000 03000000 0400 77         (15)
   a=1    b=2  pad    a=3    b=4  tail
```

The first element is padded to the element's four-byte alignment, the
second is not, and the octet lands at offset 14. Cyclone and Fast DDS
prefix the array's delimiter under XCDR2 for 19 bytes; RTI does not,
per the disagreement below.

### An inherited member is written first, and the ids run on

Run on 2026-08-09. Cases `struct_inherit`, `struct_inherit_app` and
`struct_inherit_mut`.

```idl
@final struct Base   { long base_a; short base_b; };
@final struct Sample : Base { double derived_a; octet derived_b; };
```

Cyclone and RTI, both versions:

```
7929edff feff 0000 182d4454fb210940 ab      (17)
 base_a  b_b  pad      derived_a     d_b
```

The base's members lead, the derived type's follow, and the base gets no
frame of its own — one flat run, which is XTypes 1.3 §7.4.1.1.5.1's "as
if all of the members had been defined, in the same order, in the
most-derived type". With `@appendable` on both, the same run behind one
`11000000` delimiter for 21 bytes: the base does not get a second one.

The `@mutable` pair is what settles the member ids. Cyclone under XCDR2:

```
21000000 00000020 7929edff 01000010 feff 0000
DHEADER  id=0 lc2  base_a   id=1 lc1  b_b  pad
         02000030 182d4454fb210940 03000000 ab
         id=2 lc3     derived_a    id=3 lc0 d_b
```

RTI writes the same 37 bytes, differing only in the padding after `feff`
(`0800` against Cyclone's `0000`). Those two octets are the probe's
buffer, not RTI's output: RTI's serialiser writes nothing at a fill
position, and its RTPS layer writes zero there — `tools/wire-capture`.
Cyclone's `0000` is Cyclone's, written in `dds_cdrstream.c:343`. The
derived type's first member is id **2**, not id 0 — the ids continue
across the boundary, as §7.3.1.2.1.1 requires.

### A derived structure that states no extensibility is framed as its base

Case `struct_inherit_mut_silent`.

```idl
@mutable struct Base { long base_a; short base_b; };
struct Sample : Base { double derived_a; octet derived_b; };
```

Cyclone and RTI write the same bytes as for the `@mutable` pair: under
XCDR2 the 37 bytes above, DHEADER and one EMHEADER per member; under
XCDR1 Cyclone's 72-byte parameter list with extended PIDs and RTI's
40-byte PL_CDR. `Sample` has the base's extensibility, which DDS-XTypes
1.3 §7.2.2.4.5 gives a derived structure that states none. ZeroDDS gave
it the rule's appendable default before and wrote a DHEADER with no
EMHEADERs (`crates/wire-probe/tests/vendor_bytes.rs`,
`a_derived_structure_that_states_no_extensibility_is_framed_as_its_base`).
Fast DDS and OpenDDS need a fill file of their own and have none for this
case.

### A typedef of an array is the array, flat

Run on 2026-08-09. Case `typedef_array`.

```idl
typedef long Matrix[2][3];
@final struct Sample { Matrix grid; long tail; };
```

Cyclone and RTI, both versions, 28 bytes:

```
01000000 02000000 03000000 ffffffff ffffff7f 7929edff ffffffff
```

Six `long`s in row-major order and then the tail — the typedef is
transparent and, the element being primitive, the array takes no
delimiter under XCDR2 either.

### An enumerator's holder is signed, and the bound is a width

Run on 2026-08-09. Cases `enum_negative` and `enum_bb8_200`. Neither
case has three implementations behind it, because each is one the other
refuses to compile — which is itself the finding.

```idl
enum Signed { @value(-1) MINUS, @value(0) ZERO, @value(2147483647) MAX };
@final struct Sample { Signed first; Signed second; };
```

| | |
|---|---|
| RTI, both versions | `ffffffff ffffff7f` (8) |
| Cyclone | refuses: ``@value(-1) cannot be applied to 'enumerator' element`` |

`-1` is `ffffffff`, the two's complement — the holder is Int32 and
signed, per the ENUM_TYPE entry of §7.4.3.5.

```idl
@bit_bound(8) enum Small { @value(3) RED, @value(9) GREEN, @value(200) BLUE };
@final struct Sample { Small first; Small second; octet tail; };
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Cyclone, both versions | `c8 09 ab` (3) |
| RTI | refuses: `Only 32 bit bounds are accepted for enumerations.` |

`200` is `c8`: Cyclone reads `@bit_bound(8)` as a width and accepts any
value expressible in eight bits, not only the Int8 range. Taken
together the two runs fix the accepted range at `-2^(n-1) ..= 2^n - 1`.

### A union may switch on an enumeration

Run on 2026-08-09. Cases `union_enum` and `union_enum_qual`.

```idl
enum Colour { RED, GREEN, BLUE };
union Choice switch (Colour) {
    case RED: long whole;
    case GREEN:
    case BLUE: double fraction;
};
@final struct Sample { Choice picked; long tail; };
```

| | XCDR1 | XCDR2 |
|---|---|---|
| Cyclone | `01000000 00000000 182d4454fb210940 ffffffff` (20) | `01000000 182d4454fb210940 ffffffff` (16) |
| RTI | identical (20) | `0c000000` then the same (20) |

The discriminator is the enumerator's value, written in the holder its
bit bound calls for. The XCDR2 split is the default-extensibility
disagreement below and nothing else: `Choice` is unannotated, RTI reads
it as appendable and delimits it, Cyclone reads it as final.

`union_enum_qual` writes the same union with the enumeration in a module
and the labels as `m::RED`, `m::GREEN`, `m::BLUE` — the form IDL 4.2
§7.4.1.4.2 gives. RTI produced the same bytes as above. Cyclone's `idlc`
accepted and generated the IDL; only the harness's own `fill.inc` failed
to compile, because Cyclone mangles the enumerator to `m_GREEN` and the
shared fill says `GREEN`. Neither vendor requires the enumeration's own
name in the path.

### Length codes 5, 6 and 7, and which members reach them

Run on 2026-08-09. Case `mut_lengthcodes`. Nothing in the corpus reached
these three codes before this run, so the writer, the reader and the
NEXTINT fix behind them stood on §7.4.3.4.2 and on each other.

```idl
@final struct Cell { long a; long b; };
@mutable struct LenCodes {
    string s; sequence<octet> o1; sequence<short> s2;
    sequence<long> l4; sequence<double> d8; sequence<Cell> sc;
    Cell arr[2]; long ap[2]; Cell nested; long tail;
};
```

with `s="abc"`, `o1=[1,2,3]`, `s2=[-1,2]`, `l4=[1,2]`, `d8=[1.5]`,
`sc=[{1,2}]`, `arr=[{3,4},{5,6}]`, `ap=[7,8]`, `nested={9,10}`,
`tail=11`. The EMHEADER each member gets under XCDR2, little endian:

| member | Cyclone | RTI | Fast DDS |
|---|---|---|---|
| `string s` | `00000050` **LC5** | `00000050` **LC5** | `00000050` **LC5** |
| `sequence<octet> o1` | `01000050` **LC5** | `01000050` **LC5** | `01000050` **LC5** |
| `sequence<short> s2` | `02000040` LC4 | `02000040` LC4 | `02000030` LC3 |
| `sequence<long> l4` | `03000060` **LC6** | `03000060` **LC6** | `03000060` **LC6** |
| `sequence<double> d8` | `04000070` **LC7** | `04000070` **LC7** | `04000070` **LC7** |
| `sequence<Cell> sc` | `05000050` **LC5** | `05000040` LC4 | `05000050` **LC5** |
| `Cell arr[2]` | `06000050` **LC5** | `06000040` LC4 | `06000050` **LC5** |
| `long ap[2]` | `07000040` LC4 | `07000040` LC4 | `07000030` LC3 |
| `Cell nested` | `08000040` LC4 | `08000040` LC4 | `08000030` LC3 |
| `long tail` | `09000020` LC2 | `09000020` LC2 | `09000020` LC2 |

All three reach LC5, LC6 and LC7, and on the same members. The word
behind each of the three is the member's own: LC5 over `04000000` and
then `abc\0`, LC6 over the count `02000000` for eight bytes of `long`,
LC7 over the count `01000000` for eight bytes of `double`. Byte totals
including the DHEADER: Cyclone 160, RTI 160, Fast DDS 148.

Under XCDR1 there are no length codes and the three shapes are
divergence 2 below: Cyclone 224 bytes with `PID_EXTENDED` throughout,
RTI and Fast DDS 144 with the short form.

**The rule the codes follow is "reuse the leading word when there is
one".** A string, a sequence of one-byte elements, and any collection
that carries a DHEADER all begin with a four-byte word that is the byte
length of what follows, so LC5 costs nothing. A sequence of four- or
eight-byte primitives begins with a count, which is that length divided
by four or eight, so LC6 and LC7 cost nothing either. A sequence of
two-byte elements has neither, and takes LC4.

Where RTI parts is not the codes but divergence 1: it writes no
collection DHEADER, so on `sc` and `arr` there is no leading length word
to reuse and LC4 with an explicit NEXTINT is the only code left. Its
NEXTINT is the same number Cyclone's DHEADER holds, so the two streams
differ in one nibble and in nothing else.

**This run found a defect.** `zerodds_ast_layout::length_code` had no
arm for an array and fell through to a size-based fallback, which gave
LC4 *and* still wrote the DHEADER: `06000040 14000000 10000000` and then
the elements, four bytes longer than any of the three. It also gave LC5
to a `map<long, long>`, whose leading word is an entry count and not a
byte length. Both are fixed and the corpus case
`tests/interop-corpus/struct-mutable-length-codes` is this type.

### Which short code a member that could take one takes

The split in the table above on `s2`, `ap` and `nested` is a choice, not
a rule. LC0 to LC3 state a member's byte length in the header itself and
are available whenever that length is 1, 2, 4 or 8; LC4 states it in a
following word and is always available. Fast DDS takes the short code
whenever the member happens to fit — including for an eight-byte
`sequence<short>`, which it can only know per sample. Cyclone takes LC4
for a nested aggregate and for an array of primitives whatever their
size, with a `FIXME` beside it. Both decode.

A static layout plan cannot make Fast DDS's choice for a sequence: the
count is a runtime value. It can and does make it for a fixed-size array
and for a nested aggregate, which is why this project's `ap` and
`nested` read `07000030` and `08000030`.

### A nested aggregate that carries a DHEADER

Run on 2026-08-09. Case `mut_lc_nested`.

```idl
@appendable struct ACell { long a; long b; };
@mutable   struct MCell { long a; long b; };
@final     struct Cell  { long a; long b; };
enum Colour { RED, GREEN, BLUE };
@mutable struct LenNest {
    ACell app; MCell mnest; Colour ce[2]; Cell arr1[1]; long tail;
};
```

| member | Cyclone | RTI | Fast DDS |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ACell app` | `00000040` LC4 | `00000050` **LC5** | `00000050` **LC5** |
| `MCell mnest` | `01000040` LC4 | `01000050` **LC5** | `01000050` **LC5** |
| `Colour ce[2]` | `02000050` **LC5** | `02000040` LC4 | `02000030` LC3 |
| `Cell arr1[1]` | `03000050` **LC5** | `03000040` LC4 | `03000050` **LC5** |
| `long tail` | `04000020` LC2 | `04000020` LC2 | `04000020` LC2 |

An `@appendable` or `@mutable` nested member begins with its own
DHEADER, so the same "reuse the leading word" reading gives LC5, and RTI
and Fast DDS both take it. Cyclone does not, and says why in
`dds_cdrstream.c`: `case DDS_OP_VAL_UNI: case DDS_OP_VAL_EXT: return
LENGTH_CODE_NEXTINT; /* FIXME: may be optimized for specific cases, e.g.
when EXT type is appendable */`. Two of three against one, both
decodable, four bytes apart. This project writes Cyclone's LC4 and its
bytes for `LenNest` are Cyclone's byte for byte; the majority form is an
open item rather than a silent change, because it moves recorded bytes
for every `@mutable` type holding a delimited aggregate.

`Colour ce[2]` is divergence 1 again, seen from the length-code side:
Cyclone delimits an array of enumerations and reuses the delimiter, Fast
DDS delimits neither and states the eight bytes in the code, RTI writes
the NEXTINT.

### A collection of bitmasks is delimited by Cyclone and not by Fast DDS

Run on 2026-08-09. Case `mut_lc_enum`. `rtiddsgen` does not parse
`bitmask` in IDL at all, so there are two rows.

```idl
enum Colour { RED, GREEN, BLUE };
@bit_bound(16) bitmask Flags { @position(0) a, @position(3) b };
@mutable struct LenEnum { sequence<Colour> cs; sequence<Flags> fs; long tail; };
```

| | `sequence<Colour>` | `sequence<Flags>` |
|---|---|---|
| Cyclone | `00000050` **LC5** over DHEADER `0c000000` | `01000050` **LC5** over DHEADER `08000000` |
| Fast DDS | `00000060` **LC6** over the count `02000000` | `01000030` LC3 over eight bytes |

Fast DDS exempts a bitmask collection from the delimiter exactly as it
exempts an enumeration one. Until this run nothing measured said what a
vendor did with a collection of bitmasks, and
`CollectionDelimiterPolicy::EnumIsPrimitive` deliberately covered only
the enumeration; it now covers both, which is what the policy's name
already claimed.

## Where the vendors disagree

Each of these needs a policy, because there is no set of bytes that all
three accept.

### 1. Collection delimiter for non-primitive elements

XTypes 1.3 §7.4.3.5 rule (9) for arrays and rule (12) for sequences: a
collection whose element type is not primitive carries a `DHEADER`
under XCDR2. Rules (8) and (11) exempt collections of primitives.
§7.2.2.2 defines the primitive types; an enumeration is a constructed
type under §7.2.2.4.1, so it is not one.

| case | element | Cyclone | RTI | Fast DDS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `array_nested` | `@final struct Cell` | 20, delimiter `10000000` | 16, none | 20, delimiter |
| `seq_struct` | `@final struct Cell` | 24, delimiter `14000000` | 20, none | 24, delimiter |
| `seq_appendable` | `@appendable struct ACell` | 32, delimiter `1c000000` | 28, none | 32, delimiter |
| `array_enum` | `enum Colour` | 12, delimiter `08000000` | 8, none | 8, none |
| `seq_enum` | `enum Colour` | 16, delimiter `0c000000` | 12, none | 12, none |

RTI omits the collection delimiter in every case, including
`seq_appendable`, where it still writes the per-element `08000000`
delimiters the element's own extensibility calls for. So it is the
collection-level rule RTI does not implement, not delimiting in
general.

Fast DDS writes it for aggregates and omits it for enumerations. The
spec's own rationale for the exemption reads "these sequences are
intrinsically delimited in the sense that the CDR representation allows
determining the serialized size of the entire sequence without
iterating over each element", which is true of a fixed-width enum —
Fast DDS follows the rationale, Cyclone follows the letter.

Only Cyclone matches the specification on all five rows.

### 2. PL_CDR1 member headers

```idl
@mutable struct Ext { long a; double b; short c; };   // 7, 1.5, -3
```

XCDR1:

```
cyclone  017f0800 00000000 04000000 07000000
         017f0800 01000000 08000000 0000000000 00f83f
         017f0800 02000000 04000000 fdff0000
         027f0000                                        (56)

rti      00000400 07000000
         01000800 0000000000 00f83f
         02000400 fdff0000
         027f0000                                        (32)

fastdds  00000400 07000000
         01000800 0000000000 00f83f
         02000200 fdff 0000
         023f0000                                        (32)
```

Three streams, three shapes:

- Cyclone writes `PID_EXTENDED` (`0x3f01`, with the must-understand bit
  set, so `0x7f01` in the stream) for every member and puts the member id
  and length in the eight bytes that follow. It never uses the short
  form. Read from `dds_stream_write_sampleLE`; whether Cyclone's RTPS
  layer rewrites a PL_CDR1 header on the way out has not been captured.
- RTI uses the short form and rounds each member's declared length up
  to the alignment — `short c` gets length 4.
- Fast DDS uses the short form with the member's own length — `short c`
  gets length 2, and the two padding bytes before the sentinel are not
  counted in it.

They also disagree on the sentinel: Cyclone and RTI write `027f0000`,
`PID_LIST_END` with the must-understand bit; Fast DDS writes `023f0000`
without it.

Under XCDR2 all three produce the same 30 bytes,
`1a000000 00000020 07000000 01000030 0000000000 00f83f 02000010 fdff`.

#### The member's own must-understand bit

```idl
@mutable struct M { @id(1) @must_understand long a; @id(2) long b; };
```

`a = 7`, `b = -2`, little endian. Case `mut_mustunderstand`.

```
cyclone  017f0800 010000|40| 04000000 07000000
         017f0800 02000000 04000000 feffffff
         027f0000                                        (36)

rti      01|40|0400 07000000
         02000400 feffffff
         027f0000                                        (20)

fastdds  01000400 07000000
         02000400 feffffff
         023f0000                                        (20)
```

§7.4.1.2.2: `FLAG_MUST_UNDERSTAND` "shall be set if and only if the
must_understand property of the member is set to true". Cyclone and RTI
do; Fast DDS writes the bare id and the flag is nowhere in its stream.

**The bit is in a different place in each form, and Cyclone shows why
that matters.** In the short header it is bit 14 of the sixteen-bit id —
RTI's `0140`. In the extended header it is `FLAG_2` (`0x40000000`) of
the 32-bit `eMemberHeader`, §7.4.1.2.1 — Cyclone's `01000040` for the
member that declares it, against `02000000` for the plain member beside
it in the same sample. The *marker* `017f` also carries a
must-understand bit, and Cyclone sets it on every parameter it writes,
so a reader that took the member's property from the marker would treat
the whole list as must-understand.

This project wrote no member flag at all and, worse, read the extended
`eMemberHeader` as a bare 32-bit id: Cyclone's member arrived with id
`0x40000001`, matched nothing the model declares, and — because an
unmatched XCDR1 parameter was skipped rather than refused — was
**silently dropped**.

Under XCDR2 the same property is `M_FLAG`, bit 31 of the EMHEADER, and
there the split is the other way: Cyclone and RTI write `010000a0` and
Fast DDS writes `01000020`. That is I11 and is unchanged.

### 3. Default extensibility

The IDL from GitHub issues #41 and #42, unannotated throughout:

```idl
module common {
    module util {
        struct Location    { double x; double y; double z; };
        struct Orientation { double x; double y; double z; };
    };
    struct Robot {
        ::common::util::Location location;
        ::common::util::Orientation orientation;
    };
};
```

| | XCDR1 | XCDR2 |
|---|---|---|
| Cyclone | 48, no delimiter | 48, no delimiter |
| RTI | 48, no delimiter | 60: `38000000` then `18000000` + 24 bytes twice |

Cyclone read the types as `@final`, RTI as `@appendable`. XTypes 1.3
§7.3.1.2.1.8 settles which is correct:

> In the event that the representation of a given type does not
> indicate the type's extensibility kind, the type shall be considered
> appendable. Implementations may provide a mechanism to override this
> default behavior; for example, IDL compilers may provide
> configuration options to allow users to specify whether types of
> unspecified extensibility are to be considered final, appendable, or
> mutable.

Cyclone's `idlc` agrees, in a warning it prints for this file:

> No default extensibility provided. For one or more of the aggregated
> types in the IDL the extensibility is not explicitly set. Currently
> the default extensibility for these types is 'final', but this may
> change to 'appendable' in a future release because that is the
> default in the DDS XTypes specification.

`-Wno-implicit-extensibility` silences the warning without changing the
default. `idlc` has no option to change it; the IDL has to be
annotated.

Fast DDS could not be measured on this case: `fastddsgen` rejects the
root-anchored member type.

```
gen.idl:17:8: error: '::' was not defined previously
gen.idl:18:8: error: '::' was not defined previously
```

`::common::util::Location` is the fully scoped name of OMG IDL 4.2
§7.5.2 and is valid. `crates/idl-lower/tests/reported_idl.rs` holds
this IDL as a fixture.

### 4. `wstring` length, character width and terminator

```idl
@final struct WStr { wstring w; octet tail; };   // tail = 0xAB
```

filled twice: `w = "ab"`, and `w = "𝄞"` — `U+1D11E`, outside the Basic
Multilingual Plane, which is where a character count and a byte count
stop being two spellings of the same thing.

The C element type differs per vendor and the fill does too: Cyclone's
member is `wchar_t *`, RTI's is `DDS_Wchar *` (sixteen bits, so the
non-BMP character is supplied as its surrogate pair), Fast DDS's is
`std::wstring`. Cases `wstring_member` and `wstring_nonbmp`.

Little endian:

| | XCDR1 | XCDR2 |
|---|---|---|
| Cyclone `"ab"` | `04000000 61006200 ab` (9) | identical (9) |
| RTI `"ab"` | `03000000 61000000 62000000 00000000 ab` (17) | `04000000 61006200 ab` (9) |
| Fast DDS `"ab"` | `02000000 61006200 ab` (9) | identical (9) |
| Cyclone `"𝄞"` | `04000000 34d81edd ab` (9) | identical (9) |
| RTI `"𝄞"` | `03000000 34d80000 1edd0000 00000000 ab` (17) | `04000000 34d81edd ab` (9) |
| Fast DDS `"𝄞"` | `01000000 1ed1 ab` (7) | identical (7) |

Three forms:

- **Cyclone in both versions, RTI under XCDR2** — the length is the
  byte count, the characters are UTF-16 code units, there is no
  terminator, and a code point outside the BMP is a surrogate pair
  counting four. This is XTypes 1.3 §7.4.1.1.2, "This is twice the
  number of characters in the string", with §7.4.3.5.3 rule (4)'s "No
  NUL".
- **RTI under XCDR1** — the length is the character count *including* a
  terminating NUL, and each character is four bytes. `"ab"` is a count
  of 3 and twelve bytes of content. Nothing is lost above the BMP: both
  surrogates are written, zero-extended.
- **Fast DDS in both versions** — the length is the character count and
  each character is two bytes, with no terminator. Above the BMP the
  character is truncated to sixteen bits: `1ed1` is `U+1D11E` cut down
  to `U+D11E`.

`U+D11E` is a Hangul syllable. It is a valid code point, well-formed
UTF-16 and the right length, so a reader that gets Fast DDS's length
convention right still returns a different character than was sent and
has nothing to object to. Only a code point whose low sixteen bits fall
in `D800..=DFFF` leaves a lone surrogate a reader can refuse, and that
is luck. This is why the ZeroDDS writer refuses a non-BMP code point
under the character-count policy instead of reproducing the
truncation.

Fast DDS's shape is in its own source. Fast CDR 2.3.5,
`src/cpp/Cdr.cpp:884`, computes `wstrlen * 2` for the capacity check and
then serialises `wstrlen` — the count, not the byte length — and writes
each four-byte `wchar_t` as two bytes.

Big endian, through `gate-be` (below):

| | XCDR1 | XCDR2 |
|---|---|---|
| Cyclone `"ab"` | `00000004 61006200 ab` (9) | identical (9) |
| RTI `"ab"` | `00000003 00000061 00000062 00000000 ab` (17) | `00000004 00610062 ab` (9) |
| Fast DDS `"ab"` | `00000002 00610062 ab` (9) | identical (9) |
| Cyclone `"𝄞"` | `00000004 34d81edd ab` (9) | identical (9) |
| RTI `"𝄞"` | `00000003 0000d834 0000dd1e 00000000 ab` (17) | `00000004 d834dd1e ab` (9) |
| Fast DDS `"𝄞"` | `00000001 d11e ab` (7) | identical (7) |

The three forms are the same three. What big endian adds is a fourth
divergence that little endian cannot show:

**Cyclone does not put the code units of a `wstring` in the stream's
byte order.** Its length word swaps — `00000004` — and its content does
not: `61006200` in both orders, where RTI and Fast DDS write
`00610062`. Read as a big-endian stream, Cyclone's `"ab"` is U+6100
U+6200, two different characters, and nothing in the frame says so.

It is the `wstring` path and not the byte order generally. The scalar
`wchar` of `@final struct WCh { wchar c; octet tail; }` with
`c = U+0061`, case `wchar_member`, swaps in all three:

| | XCDR1 LE | XCDR1 BE | XCDR2 LE | XCDR2 BE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cyclone | `6100 ab` | `0061 ab` | `6100 ab` | `0061 ab` |
| RTI | `61000000 ab` | `00000061 ab` | `6100 ab` | `0061 ab` |
| Fast DDS | `6100 ab` | `0061 ab` | `6100 ab` | `0061 ab` |

That row also records RTI's four-byte `wchar` under XCDR1, which is the
same character width its XCDR1 `wstring` uses.

ZeroDDS writes the specification's form and the stream's byte order, so
it agrees with Cyclone and RTI-XCDR2 in little endian and with RTI and
Fast DDS in big endian. `WstringLengthPolicy` in
`crates/ast-layout/src/key.rs` selects the other two length forms and
carries the argument for why the reader takes a configured form rather
than inferring one. Cyclone's unswapped big-endian content has no
policy: it is recorded here and not modelled.

### 5. The KeyHash of a keyless type, and of a `@mutable` keyed one

Measured on 2026-08-09 through purpose-built probes under
`tools/keyhash-probe/` on the Linux host — Cyclone DDS 11.0.1, RTI
Connext 7.7.0 with rtiddsgen 4.7.0, Fast DDS from source — plus `tcpdump`
on `lo` for the wire rows. `run-all.sh` redoes the offline probes and
`run-wire.sh` the captures.

```idl
@final   struct Foo          { @key long id; long x; long y; };   // id = 0x12345678
@mutable struct FooMutable   { @key long id; long x; long y; };
@final   struct NoKeyFinal   { long a; long b; };
@mutable struct NoKeyMutable { long a; long b; };
```

**The keyed control.** All three give §9.6.4.8 Example 1's sixteen bytes,
`12345678 00000000 00000000 00000000`, and all three put them in
PID_KEY_HASH on the wire. RTI reproduces them under CDR_BE, PL_CDR_BE,
CDR2_BE, D_CDR2_BE and PL_CDR2_BE alike.

**A keyless type has no KeyHash anywhere.** No vendor computes one and
none emits PID_KEY_HASH for a keyless topic.

| | how it decides | on the wire |
|---|---|---|
| Cyclone | `idlc` emits `m_nkeys = 0`; `fix_serdata_default_nokey` never calls `gen_serdata_key`, so `serdata_default_get_keyhash` asserts on `KEYBUFTYPE_UNSET` | writer entityId `0x00000203` (`WRITER_NO_KEY`), no inline QoS. Gated twice: `ddsi_transmit.c` needs `num_readers_requesting_keyhash > 0` and `ddsi_endpoint.c` counts only `WRITER_WITH_KEY`. `GenerateKeyhash` defaults to `false` and its own help text says "for topics with keys" |
| RTI | `get_key_kind` returns `PRES_TYPEPLUGIN_NO_KEY`; the vtable carries rtiddsgen's own comment that `instanceToKeyHashFnc`, `serializedSampleToKeyHashFnc` and `serializedKeyToKeyHashFnc` "are only used for keyed types" and sets all three to NULL. No `KeyHolder` typedef is generated | entityId `0x80000003`, no inline QoS |
| Fast DDS | `is_compute_key_provided = false`; the generated `compute_key` discards its arguments and returns false | entityId `0x00000103`, no inline QoS. `DataMsg.hpp` guards `add_parameter_key` on `WITH_KEY == topicKind` |

Measured with a handle pre-filled `0xAA`, Fast DDS returns false and
leaves all sixteen bytes `0xAA`, with `force_md5` false and true alike.

Two counterfactuals are worth keeping, because they are what the literal
reading of Step 1 looks like when you reach past the decision.

- Cyclone's own `dds_stream_extract_keyBE_from_key` over the empty key
  buffer `gen_serdata_key` would produce gives
  `d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e`, the MD5 of the empty string, for
  `NoKeyFinal` under XCDR1 and XCDR2 and for `NoKeyMutable` under XCDR2.
  No `@final`-versus-`@mutable` split of any kind.
- RTI's XCDR interpreter, driven directly past the plugin,
  *does* implement the literal reading:
  `PRESTypePlugin_interpretedSerializeKeyForKeyhash` on `NoKeyFinal`
  returns `12345678 00000014` — every member. The plugin never reaches
  it.

So the clause's "Otherwise, do not remove any members" is implemented in
at least one vendor's interpreter and reachable from none of them.
`crates/wire-probe/src/encode.rs::key_hash` returns `ProbeError::NoKey`.

**Where RTI diverges: a `@mutable` keyed type under XCDR1.** Cyclone and
Fast DDS force the key holder to FINAL for all three extensibilities and
give Example 1's sixteen bytes. RTI does under XCDR2 and does not under
XCDR1: the holder keeps its parameter-list framing,
`00000004 12345678 7f020000`, and `maxSizeSerializedKeyV1 = 28` exceeds
sixteen, so Step 5.2 applies and the hash is
`0482916deda7e1d2459197a743466627f`.

§9.6.4.8 Step 1 says `FooKeyHolder` "shall have extensibility kind
'FINAL'", so Example 1's bytes are the specification's answer and RTI's
XCDR1 form is a dialect. ZeroDDS writes the specification's answer —
`extensibility_of` returns `Final` under `Purpose::Key`. Whether
`Dialect` should carry RTI's XCDR1 key holder as a fourth answer is open;
`docs/OPEN-ITEMS.md` has it.

### 6. How deep Step 1's member removal reaches

Measured on 2026-08-09 through the same `tools/keyhash-probe/` harness,
extended with the shapes below. XTypes 1.3 §7.6.8 Step 1 is one sentence
with two halves:

> If there are any key members, then remove the non-key members from
> FooKeyHolder. Otherwise do not remove any members.

and Step 3 applies steps 1 and 2 "recursively to the members of
FooKeyHolder if they are themselves AggregatedTypes". `FooKeyHolder` at
that point is whatever Step 1 left, so for a keyless aggregate it is
every member and Step 3 reaches all of them. No depth limit is written
into the clause.

```idl
@final struct NestedNoKey        { long a; long b; };            // a=0x0a0a0a0a b=0x0b0b0b0b
@final struct OuterKeylessNested { @key NestedNoKey inner; long tail; };

@final struct NestedSomeKey      { @key long a; long b; };
@final struct OuterKeyedNested   { @key NestedSomeKey inner; long tail; };

@final struct ChainLeaf          { @key long p; long q; };       // p=0x0d0d0d0d q=0x0e0e0e0e
@final struct ChainMid           { @key ChainLeaf inner; long r; };  // r=0x0f0f0f0f
@final struct ChainOuter         { @key ChainMid mid; long tail; };

@final struct DeepLeaf           { @key long p; long q; };
@final struct DeepMid            { DeepLeaf leaf; long r; };     // declares no key
@final struct DeepOuter          { @key DeepMid mid; long tail; };
```

| holder members | Cyclone X1 | Cyclone X2 | Fast DDS | RTI X1 | RTI X2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `OuterKeylessNested` | `a` `b` | `a` `b` | `a` `b` | `a` `b` | `a` `b` |
| `OuterKeyedNested` | `a` | `a` | `a` | `a` | `a` |
| `ChainOuter` | `p` | `p` | `p` | `p` | `p` |
| `DeepOuter` | `p` `r` | `p` `r` | `p` `r` | `p` `q` `r` | `p` `r` |

**All five combinations implement the second half of the sentence.**
`OuterKeylessNested` puts both of `NestedNoKey`'s members in the holder —
Cyclone reports `nkeys = 2`, RTI `maxSizeSerializedKey 8 / 8`, Fast DDS
`0a0a0a0a0b0b0b0b` zero-extended. A `@key` member of a keyless type
contributes all of that type's members, not none.

**Recursion through keyed levels is unlimited everywhere.** `ChainOuter`
is keyed at all three levels and every combination gives `p` alone.

**RTI under XCDR1 stops at the first keyless level.** `DeepOuter` has a
keyless `DeepMid` above a keyed `DeepLeaf`. Cyclone, Fast DDS and RTI's
own XCDR2 holder keep applying Step 1 below the keyless level and drop
`q`; RTI's XCDR1 holder takes `DeepMid` whole and keeps it.
`maxSizeSerializedKey V1 / V2` reports `12 / 8` for that one type, so the
two are different holders and not one holder serialized twice.

`KeyHolderNesting` carries the divergence and `Dialect::key_holder_nesting`
selects it, under XCDR1 only. The default is `Recursive`: the clause, and
four of the five combinations.

**The corpus case.** `tests/interop-corpus/combined-everything` is the
same question on a larger type, and both measurable vendors agree with
the recursive reading:

```idl
@final     struct CombLeaf   { @key long k; short v; };           // k=-1234567 v=-2
@appendable struct CombMiddle { CombLeaf leaf; sequence<string> names; };
@mutable   struct CombSample { @key CombMiddle middle; long tail; };
```

with `names = ["", "über ሴ"]`. Cyclone reports `nkeys = 2` and serializes
`ffed2979` for `k` followed by the whole `names` sequence — `v` and
`tail` are gone, so the keyless `CombMiddle` contributed both its members
and the keyed `CombLeaf` below it was filtered to `k`. RTI's XCDR2 holder
has the same member set. The two differ only by RTI's collection
delimiter, which is divergence 1 above and already a dialect:

| | holder bytes |
|---|---|
| Cyclone XCDR2 | `ffed2979` `0000001a` `00000002` `00000001 00` `000000` `0000000a` `c3bc626572 20e188b4 00` |
| RTI XCDR2 | `ffed2979` `00000002` `00000001 00` `000000` `0000000a` `c3bc626572 20e188b4 00` |
| RTI XCDR1 | `00000024` `ffed2979` `fffe` `0000` `00000002` … — `v` kept, as `KeylessNestedWhole` says |

Cyclone's MD5 of its holder is `80208c54a0b66e6ef9dbf93e7dbc3ac1`, which
is what `combined-everything`'s README now records. The corpus case
`annotation-key-whole-struct` — `@final struct Inner { long a; short b; }`
under `@key Inner inner` — gives `ffed2979fffe` zero-extended on all
three vendors, and that is its recorded row.

**Fast DDS cannot compute this one.** `CombSamplePubSubType::compute_key`
throws `eprosima::fastcdr::exception::NotEnoughMemoryException` out of a
`noexcept` frame and the process aborts: fastddsgen sizes the key buffer
from `CombSample_max_key_cdr_typesize`, 20, which leaves the unbounded
`sequence<string>` out, and this holder is 34 octets. Every bounded shape
above computes normally. The row is absent from the table above rather
than guessed; the probe runs the type in a child process, which ends on
signal 6.

**With `names = []` all three computed it**, the holder then fitting the
20 octets. Cyclone XCDR2 serializes `ffed2979` `00000004` `00000000` and
Fast DDS gives the same MD5, `c14ff8ae1e3185d9e12d88af6b1a1458`: the
sequence keeps its DHEADER in the holder. RTI XCDR2 serializes
`ffed2979` `00000000`, MD5 `81485919ce1f729031bd5438ec2372f2`, divergence
1 again. `crates/wire-probe/tests/key_holder_alignment.rs` asserts both.

### 7. `@hashid`, and the ids around it

Measured through `tools/wireprobe/` on the same host. Every case is a
`@mutable struct Sample` under `--encoding xcdr2 --endian le`, so each
member's id reaches the wire in its EMHEADER and can be read back out of
the payload; the ids below are `word & 0x0FFFFFFF` of each header.

**The clause.** DDS-XTypes 1.3 §7.3.1.2.1.1:

> The computation of a Member ID from a string value, whether the string
> is the member name (e.g. when using @autoid(HASH) or @hashid without
> parameters), or an explicit string parameter (e.g. when using @hashid
> with a string parameter), shall use the following algorithm:
> 1. Compute a 4-byte hash of the string as specified in 7.2.2.4.4.4.5.
> 2. Interpret the resulting 4-byte has as a Little Endian unsigned
>    32-bit integer.
> 3. Perform a bitwise AND operation with the integer 0x0FFFFFFF to zero
>    the most significant 4-bits of the integer.

and §7.2.2.4.4.4.5:

> Unless otherwise noted, the 4-byte hashes computed from strings shall
> consist of the first 4 bytes of the MD5 hash of the UTF-8 encoding of
> the string, without any 'nul' terminator.

The same clause names which string goes in: "If the annotation is used
without any parameter or with the empty string as a parameter, then the
Member ID shall be computed from the member name." Two of them may not
be combined: "At most one of these two annotations may appear on a
member. Otherwise it shall be considered an error."

There is no room in that for a second reading, and §7.3.1.2.1.1 works
two hashes out by hand as Example 2 — `ID(color) = 0x0FA5DD70`,
`ID(size) = 0x047790DA` for `@hashid("shapesize") long size`. Those two
are the oracle used below; the resolution that introduced the algorithm
is OMG issue DDSXTY13-2, which gives the same worked example and the
same little-endian step.

**Hand computation.** `md5("color")` begins `70 dd a5 df`; read
little-endian that is `0xDFA5DD70`, and masked `0x0FA5DD70`.
`md5("shapesize")` begins `da 90 77 14` → `0x147790DA` → `0x047790DA`.
Reading the same four bytes big-endian instead gives `0x00DDA5DF` and
`0x0A907714`, which is what this project produced until this
measurement.

**Measured.** Ids per member, in declaration order:

| case | IDL | hand-computed | Cyclone | RTI | Fast DDS | ZeroDDS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the clause's Example 2 | `@hashid long color; @hashid("shapesize") long size;` | `0FA5DD70` `047790DA` | same | same | same | same |
| no argument | `@hashid long alpha; @hashid long beta; long plain;` | `0343172C` `00CA7B98` `00CA7B99` | same | `0343172C` `00CA7B98` **`00000000`** | same | same |
| empty argument | `@hashid("") long alpha;` | `0343172C` | **`098C1DD4`** | same | same | same |
| argument = the member name | `@hashid("alpha") long alpha;` | `0343172C` | same | same | same | same |
| argument ≠ the member name | `@hashid("alpha") long renamed;` | `0343172C` | same | same | same | same |
| a 96-character name | `@hashid long a_member_name_…_x;` | `09B2A269` | same | same | same | same |
| non-ASCII argument | `@hashid("größe") long size;` | `063ABBFD` | same | same | same | same |
| colliding pair | `@hashid("m9852") long a; @hashid("m12254") long b;` | both `0BE17DB5`, ill-formed | refused | **accepted, both `0BE17DB5`** | refused | refused |
| both annotations | `@id(7) @hashid("alpha") long a;` | ill-formed | refused | **accepted, `0343172C`** | refused | refused |

`@autoid` takes the same derivation and every implementation agrees on
it: `@autoid(HASH)` over `color` and `size` gives `0FA5DD70 0760BDF7` in
all four, `@autoid(SEQUENTIAL)` gives `00000000 00000001` in all four,
and `@autoid(HASH)` with an `@id(10)` in the middle gives
`0FA5DD70 0000000A 0760BDF7` in all four.

The colliding pair is `m9852` and `m12254`, whose digests begin
`b5 7d e1 ab` and `b5 7d e1 5b`. The 4-byte hashes differ; the ids do
not, because little-endian puts the differing nibble in the high nibble
the mask clears. Under a big-endian reading they stay apart, which is
why this pair also tells the two readings apart without looking at the
number at all.

**Verdicts.**

- **Cyclone DDS** — right on the derivation, and its `src/idl/src/hashid.c`
  quotes the clause. Wrong on one thing: `@hashid("")` hashes the empty
  string rather than the member name, because `annotate_hashid` tests
  whether a parameter is present and not whether it is empty. Cyclone
  had the endianness bug itself, reported as
  eclipse-cyclonedds/cyclonedds#976 and fixed in 2021 by commit
  `de4ef33`; its test suite now carries both of the clause's examples.
- **RTI Connext 7.7** — right on the derivation and on the empty
  argument. Wrong on both of the rules around it: it accepts a member-id
  collision instead of rejecting the type, and it accepts `@id` and
  `@hashid` together instead of refusing them. It also does not let a
  hashed id advance the sequential counter — see below.
- **Fast DDS** — right on everything measured. The derivation is in
  `MemberedTypeCode.calculate_member_id_`, the empty argument falls back
  to the member name, and `check_unique_member_id` refuses the colliding
  pair.
- **ZeroDDS** — was wrong on the derivation, alone among the four: it
  read the first four digest bytes big-endian. Fixed in
  `crates/idl-lower/src/complete.rs::hash_id`, which now carries the
  clause's two worked examples as tests. It also hashed `""` for
  `@hashid("")` and accepted `@id` alongside `@hashid`; both are fixed.
  The corpus rows `annotation-hashid-implicit` and
  `annotation-hashid-named` were re-recorded by running the probe.

Trackers searched for a reported defect: cyclonedds (#976, above),
cyclonedds-python (#230, `@hashid` with a string argument raises
`TypeError` — open), Fast-DDS, Fast-CDR, IDL-Parser, Fast-DDS-Gen,
OpenDDS, hdds-team/hdds and zero-objects/zero-dds have none on the
derivation. OMG DDSXTY14-8 is open against §7.2.2.4.4.4.4 for leaving
behind a sentence reserving ids above `0x0FFFBFFF`, which the algorithm
introduced by DDSXTY13-2 does not honour; no implementation measured
here honours it either.

**The sequential counter after a hashed id.** Two sentences of
§7.3.1.2.1.1 disagree with each other. One says member ids follow "a
progression that starts from the most-recently specified ID (using the
@id annotation defined in Sub Clause 8.3.1.2 in [IDL])", naming only
`@id`; the other says the sequential value "shall equal to the member ID
of the previous member of the same Aggregated Type plus one", naming the
previous member whatever gave it its id. Measured:

| IDL | Cyclone | RTI | Fast DDS | ZeroDDS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `@id(10) long a; long b;` | `0000000A` `0000000B` | same | same | same |
| `@hashid long alpha; long b;` | `0343172C` `0343172D` | `0343172C` **`00000000`** | `0343172C` `0343172D` | `0343172C` `0343172D` |
| `@id(10) long a; @hashid long alpha; long b;` | `0000000A` `0343172C` `0343172D` | `0000000A` `0343172C` **`0000000B`** | as Cyclone | as Cyclone |

RTI implements the first sentence: a `@hashid` id does not advance the
counter, so an unannotated member after one continues from the last
`@id` — or from zero when there was none. The other three implement the
second. This is what puts `Sample.plain` in the `unread` and `different`
rows of `vendor_roundtrip.md` for every pair involving RTI on
`annotation-hashid-implicit`, and it is a byte difference a peer has to
match. It is **not** carried as a dialect: member ids are assigned by the
frontend in `crates/idl-lower/src/complete.rs`, and `Dialect` is a
`LayoutKey` policy that the planner consults after the ids already
exist. Making it selectable means a member-id policy the lowering pass
can see, which is a public-API change to `lower`. Recorded in
`docs/OPEN-ITEMS.md`.

Cyclone's `@hashid("")` is likewise not a dialect. It changes bytes, but
only for a construct whose sole meaning is "the same as `@hashid`" — no
vendor test suite writes it, and the plumbing it would need is the same
plumbing the RTI item needs.

## Where the three cannot answer

Three constructs the byte gate's three implementations cannot be asked,
because at most one of them parses the declaration. Measured on
2026-08-09 against a fourth DDS implementation and two CORBA ORBs.

### `map`, and the contradiction inside §7.4.3.5.3

Neither `idlc` nor `rtiddsgen` has the `map` keyword — `gen.idl:2:5:
syntax error` and `no viable alternative at input '<'` under every
language binding either offers. Fast DDS parses it in C++, and OpenDDS
3.34.0 parses it in `opendds_idl`. That is two implementations, and they
do not agree.

The clause says the shape twice. §7.4.1.1.4 makes a map equivalent to a
`sequence<MapEntry>`, which rule (12) writes as a DHEADER, then the
length, then the elements. Rule (15) writes a DHEADER and no length.
Four bytes apart, both decodable from their own DHEADER.

```idl
@final struct Cell { long a; long b; };
@final struct MapValStruct { map<long, Cell> entries; long tail; };
```

with one entry `5 -> {1, 2}` and `tail = 7`, XCDR2 little endian:

| | bytes |
|---|---|
| Fast DDS | `10000000` `01000000` `05000000 01000000 02000000` `07000000` (24) |
| OpenDDS | `0c000000` `05000000 01000000 02000000` `07000000` (20) |

**Fast DDS implements rule (12) and OpenDDS implements rule (15).** Fast
DDS's DHEADER is 16 and covers the count and the entry; OpenDDS's is 12
and covers the entry alone. Under XCDR1, where neither writes a
delimiter, both write the count and the entries and the two are
identical: `01000000 05000000 01000000 02000000 07000000`.

`map<long, sequence<long>>` through a typedef says the same, with one
entry `5 -> [1, 2]`: Fast DDS `14000000 01000000 05000000 02000000
01000000 02000000 07000000` (28), OpenDDS `10000000 05000000 02000000
01000000 02000000 07000000` (24).

Both readings are therefore in the field, which is what
`MapLengthPolicy` already carried on the strength of the clause alone.
The default, `SequenceEquivalent`, is Fast DDS's and is byte-identical
to it on `map<long,long>`, `map<long,Cell>`, `map<string,string>` and
`map<long,sequence<long>>`; `Rule15Omits` is OpenDDS's and is
byte-identical to it on the two OpenDDS could compile. Neither is a
guess any longer.

**Whether the map carries a delimiter at all is a third answer.** Rule
(14) exempts a map whose key and value are both primitive, and all three
of Fast DDS, OpenDDS and this project write `map<long, long>` as a bare
count and the pairs, in both encoding versions:
`02000000 01000000 02000000 03000000 04000000 07000000`. But Fast DDS
also omits the delimiter from `map<string, long>` —
`01000000 03000000 61620000 02000000 07000000` (20) against this
project's `10000000` and then the same (24) — while writing one for
`map<string, string>`. Its criterion is the value type alone. The
clause's own rationale for the exemption is that the size can be
determined "without iterating over each element", which a string key
defeats, so the broader reading is taken: a map is delimited unless both
halves are primitive. OpenDDS reads it the same way and emits the
delimiter branch for `map<string, long>`, though its generated code for
a string-keyed map does not compile —
`std::map<TAO::String_Manager_T<char>, int>` indexed with an
`OpenDDS::DCPS::String` — so no bytes came out of it.

OpenDDS also writes a fourth PL_CDR1 member header shape, alongside
divergence 2's three: PID 0 with flags `0xC000`, both the
must-understand bit and the implementation-specific bit set, and Fast
DDS's `023f0000` sentinel. `00c01400` and then twenty bytes, for the
primitive map above.

### `bitset`, where the field is one implementation wide

Five IDL front ends were asked for `bitset B { bitfield<3> low; };` and
four refused the keyword: Cyclone's `idlc` (`gen.idl:1:1: syntax
error`), RTI's `rtiddsgen` (`mismatched input 'bitset' expecting EOF`),
OpenDDS's `opendds_idl` and `tao_idl` (`Statement cannot be parsed`),
and omniORB's `omniidl` (`Syntax error in definition`). eProsima Fast
DDS parses it. There is no second oracle to find, and XTypes 1.3 states
no serialisation rule for the type at all — established by exhaustion in
`docs/refused-constructs.md`.

```idl
bitset B1 { bitfield<8> a; };
bitset B2 : B1 { bitfield<8> b; };
bitset B3 : B2 { bitfield<4> c; };
@final struct BitChain { octet head; B3 value; octet tail; };
```

with `head = 1, a = 0x11, b = 0x22, c = 3, tail = 0xAB`:

| | XCDR1 | XCDR2 |
|---|---|---|
| Fast DDS little endian | `01000000 11220300 ab` (9) | identical (9) |
| Fast DDS big endian | `01000000 00032211 ab` (9) | identical (9) |

Three bytes of padding after `head`, so the anchor aligns to its own
width; twenty declared bits give a four-byte anchor; the base's
bitfields take the low positions in declaration order. `fastddsgen`
flattens the chain into one struct and one `std::bitset<20>`. The
two-level `bitset Base { bitfield<3> low; }; bitset Derived : Base
{ bitfield<5> high; };` gives `8dab`, byte for byte what the same probe
gives for the two bitfields declared in one bitset.

This project now writes both, in both encodings and both byte orders.
The rule it follows where Fast DDS cannot be asked is the one XTypes
states for an inherited *structure*, §7.4.1.1.5.1 — "as if all of the
members had been defined, in the same order, in the most-derived type" —
and the `CommonBitfield` TypeObject's `unsigned short position` with its
`// Ordered by Bitfield.position`, which only round-trips if positions
run cumulatively from zero over the whole chain. That extrapolation is
written down as one above `wire_probe::encode::write_bitset`; it agrees
with the only implementation that can be measured on every case that
can be measured.

Three neighbouring cases, same run:

| case | Cyclone | RTI | Fast DDS |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bitset Wide { bitfield<40> lo; bitfield<40> hi; };` | refuses the keyword | refuses the keyword | generates `std::bitset<80>`; the link fails |
| `@bit_bound(4) bitmask Flags { @position(0) a, @position(7) b };` | `Position overflow for bit value 'b' (7), bit_bound is 4` | no `bitmask` in IDL at all | accepts; writes `80ab` |
| `bitset Narrow { bitfield<3> v; };` with `v = 200` | refuses the keyword | refuses the keyword | writes `00ab` |

Fast CDR 2.3.5 has `std::bitset<N>` overloads for `N < 9`, `< 17`, `< 33`
and `< 65` and no fifth, which is the 1/2/4/8 anchor rule arrived at
independently. The bit past the `@bit_bound` is a value §7.4.1.1.3.2
says is "not considered to be part of the bitmask", so no conforming
reader has to reconstruct it. `v = 200` in a `bitfield<3>` is narrowed
by the C++ compiler at the assignment and masked again by the generated
serialiser with `& 0x7`; 200 mod 8 is 0, and `00` goes out with no
diagnostic at either step. All three stay refused here, and the record
now says what the alternative does rather than that there is none.

### `fixed<P,S>`, measured against two CORBA ORBs

Not an XTypes type: §7.2.2 has no fixed-point kind and §7.4.3.5.3 has no
rule whose left-hand side matches. It is IDL 4.2 §7.4.1.4.4.3.4, and its
only wire definition is CORBA CDR §9.3.2.8. All three DDS generators
refuse the declaration — `gen.idl:2:5: syntax error`, `Invalid member
type`, `'fixed' . Fixed type is not supported` — and so does OpenDDS's
`tao_idl`, which reports `fixed data types are not supported` and, with
`-Wb,no_fixed_err`, emits a member with no type at all. The oracle is
therefore not a DDS vendor.

omniORB 4.3.3 is. One struct, nine members, every shape of the rule:

```idl
typedef fixed<5,2> D5S2;  typedef fixed<4,2> D4S2;  typedef fixed<3,3> D3S3;
typedef fixed<1,0> D1S0;  typedef fixed<2,0> D2S0;  typedef fixed<31,0> D31S0;
struct FixedAll {
    octet head; D5S2 pos; D5S2 neg; D5S2 zero; D4S2 even;
    D3S3 allfrac; D1S0 one; D2S0 two; D31S0 big; octet tail;
};
```

with `head=0x77`, `pos=123.45`, `neg=-123.45`, `zero=0.00`, `even=12.34`,
`allfrac=0.123`, `one=7`, `two=42`, `big=1234567890123456789012345678901`,
`tail=0xAB`:

```
omniORB   77 12345c 12345d 00000c 01234c 123c 7c 042c 1234567890123456789012345678901c ab   (35)
JacORB    77 12345c 12345d     0c 01234c 123c 7c 042c 1234567890123456789012345678901c ab   (33)
ZeroDDS   77 12345c 12345d 00000c 01234c 123c 7c 042c 1234567890123456789012345678901c ab   (35)
```

omniORB's bytes are this project's bytes, in both encoding versions and
both byte orders. Five things the run fixes:

- **Packed BCD, two digits an octet, sign in the last nibble** —
  `0xc` positive, `0xd` negative. `zero` takes `0xc`, not `0xd`.
- **The octet count comes from the declared digits, not from the
  value.** `fixed<4,2>` holding `12.34` is `01234c`: an even digit count
  gets a leading zero nibble. `fixed<2,0>` holding `42` is `042c`.
- **Alignment is one.** `head` sits at offset 0 and `pos` at offset 1,
  with no padding anywhere in the thirty-five bytes.
- **The bytes do not swap.** `--endian be` produces the same string:
  packed BCD is a byte sequence, not an integer.
- **The scale is not on the wire.** `fixed<3,3>` holding `0.123` is
  `123c`, the same three digits `fixed<3,0>` holding `123` would give.

JacORB 3.9 agrees on eight of the nine and differs on `zero`, where it
writes one octet against omniORB's three. Its `write_fixed` takes a
`BigDecimal` and no digit count, and `new BigDecimal("0.00").precision()`
is 1 in Java, so the declared width is gone by the time the ORB sees the
value. It is a property of the Java mapping and not a second reading of
the rule: for every value whose own digit count equals the declared one,
the two ORBs are byte-identical.

`omniidl` also confirms the three refusals this project makes around the
type, with its own words: `fixed<0,0>` is `Size must be at least 1`,
`fixed<2,5>` is `Fixed point scale factor is greater than the number of
digits`, and `fixed<32,0>` is `Fixed point values may not have more than
31 digits`.

### 8. The `@mutable` union, which Cyclone will not build

```idl
@mutable union Choice switch (long) {
    case 1: long whole;
    default: double frac;
};
@final struct Sample { Choice picked; long tail; };
```

`_d = 1`, `whole = 7`, `tail = -2`, little endian. Run 2026-08-09,
case `mut_union`.

| | XCDR2 | XCDR1 |
|---|---|---|
| Cyclone | `idlc`: "Mutable unions are not supported yet" | the same |
| RTI | `10000000 00000020 01000000 01000020 07000000` + `feffffff` | `00000400 01000000 01000400 07000000 027f0000` + `feffffff` |
| Fast DDS | the same | the same, sentinel `023f0000` |

Rules (27) and (28): the discriminator and the selected member each
carry an `MMEMBER` header, and under XCDR1 a `PID_LIST_END` closes the
list. Two things the clause does not fix and the two implementations
agree on:

- **The discriminator's member id is 0 and the cases run on from 1.**
  §7.3.1.2.1.1 numbers members from 0 and says nothing about a
  discriminator; both write `00000020` for it and `01000020` for the
  first case member. It is also the only numbering under which an
  implicitly numbered case member cannot collide with the
  discriminator.
- **The discriminator's `M_FLAG` is clear.** §7.2.2.4.4.4.6 says a
  discriminator's `must_understand` is always true. Neither
  implementation sets the bit, in either encoding version. The
  measurement decides and the inventory's J7 records the departure.

ZeroDDS wrote `08000000 01000000 07000000` — a DHEADER over an
undelimited discriminator and member, no headers at all, and not even
the sentinel its own planner computed. A peer parsing those bytes as
PL_CDR2 takes `01000000` for an EMHEADER with LC0 and returns a one-byte
member with no error anywhere.

## Big endian

Run on 2026-08-09 on the same host, through `tools/wireprobe/`'s three
probes rather than the byte gate — `--endian be` is the reason those
exist. Twenty-one cases and the same samples: the byte gate's set less
`struct_inherit`, `struct_inherit_app`, `struct_inherit_mut`,
`enum_negative`, `enum_bb8_200`, `union_enum` and `union_enum_qual`.
Every little-endian row those twenty-one cover was re-measured through
the probes first and came out identical, so the two harnesses agree
before the byte order is changed.

The re-measurement also filled gaps the byte gate left, because seven of
its cases carried no `fill.cpp.inc` and Fast DDS was never run on them.
Fast DDS matches the other two on `keyed`, `enumeration`, `seq_long`,
`string_member`, `union_case`, `array` and `typedef_array`, and it
produces `0000040007000000023f0000` (12) for `mut_optional` under
XCDR1 — the same short-form-plus-`023f0000` shape as `ext_mutable`.

The three `struct_inherit` cases are outside the probes' set because
`wireprobe-fill`'s C emitter writes only the derived type's members: it
reads `Ast::members_of`, which answers with a type's own members and not
its base's, and both C generators nest the base in a `parent` field
anyway. A sample filled that way comes out the right length with the
base's members zero — `0000000000000000182d4454fb210940ab` where the
section above records `7929edfffeff0000182d4454fb210940ab` — so it must
not be recorded as a measurement. The C++ emitter does walk the base
(`fastddsgen` maps inheritance to C++ inheritance, so the accessors are
flat), and the Fast DDS probe reproduces all three cases in both byte
orders, including the 37-byte `@mutable` run with id 2 on the derived
type's first member.

### What the byte order changes, and what it does not

Nothing but the byte order. For all twenty-one cases, in both encodings:

- Where the three agree in little endian they agree in big endian, and
  where they split they split into the same groups.
- Every output is the same length as its little-endian counterpart.
  Padding sits at the same offsets and reads as zero in all three — which
  for RTI and Fast DDS is the probe's buffer and not the vendor, since
  neither serialiser writes a fill octet. On the wire both write zero
  there anyway (`tools/wire-capture`), so the reading survives; the
  reason for it does not.
- No vendor changes shape: the collection delimiter, the PL_CDR1 header
  form, the sentinel and the default extensibility are the same three
  disagreements in the same three places.

The encapsulation identifier each vendor writes confirms the stream is
labelled, not merely swapped. `Point` and `Ext` through the RTI and Fast
DDS probes:

| | XCDR1 LE | XCDR1 BE | XCDR2 LE | XCDR2 BE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Point` (`@final`) | `0001` | `0000` | `0007` | `0006` |
| `Ext` (`@mutable`) | `0003` | `0002` | `000b` | `000a` |

`CDR_LE`/`CDR_BE`, `CDR2_LE`/`CDR2_BE`, `PL_CDR_LE`/`PL_CDR_BE`,
`PL_CDR2_LE`/`PL_CDR2_BE`. The parameter-list rows are the evidence that
the Fast DDS probe reads the encoding flag out of the generated
`<T>PubSubType`: a harness-chosen flag would have said `0001`/`0007`
there. Fast DDS also sets the encapsulation options word to the count of
alignment padding — `0002` for the thirty-byte `Ext` body — where RTI's
static plugin leaves it `0000`. **RTI's RTPS layer sets it**, and on a
loopback capture nobody leaves it zero over a short payload: see
`docs/wire-feature-inventory.md` B5, which retracted the reading "Fast
DDS implements it, RTI does not". Neither is part of the payload.
