### What big endian shows that little endian hides

Two fields read as a value rather than as a byte pattern only once they
are the other way round.

The PL_CDR1 member header is `{ PID, length }`, two little-endian
`unsigned short`s in `017f 0800`, which big endian spells `7f01 0008`.
The `0x7f01` Cyclone writes is `PID_EXTENDED` `0x3f01` with the
must-understand bit, and the sentinel Cyclone and RTI write is `0x7f02`
against Fast DDS's `0x3f02`; in big endian those are the leading two
bytes and readable as such. RTI's rounded length is `0004` where Fast
DDS writes `0002`, in the same position.

The XCDR2 `EMHEADER` is one `unsigned long`, and the same value:
`00000020` little endian is `20000000` big endian, both `0x20000000` —
member id 0 with length code 2. `ext_mutable`'s three headers are
`0x20000000`, `0x30000001` and `0x10000002`, which is what the
little-endian `00000020`, `01000030`, `02000010` already said.

## The CORBA column — three ORBs on the XCDR1 base

Run 2026-08-10 on the Linux test host. XCDR1 is CORBA CDR: every
alignment rule, every primitive's encoding and the string and sequence
forms are CORBA 3.3 part 2 §9.3, and XTypes 1.3 §7.4 changes them only
where it says so. This project had asked an ORB exactly once, for
`fixed<P,S>`. Three were asked here, about everything they share.

| | | writes | reads |
|---|---|---|---|
| omniORB 4.3.3 | `omniidl -bcxx` + `cdrMemoryStream` | LE and BE | LE and BE |
| TAO 2.5.24 | `tao_idl -as` + `TAO_OutputCDR` | **LE only** | LE and BE |
| JacORB 3.9 | `jacorb idl` + `CDROutputStream` | **BE only** | LE and BE |

Both write-side limits are the implementations', **at the CDR stream**.
`ACE_OutputCDR::write_4` swaps only when libACE was built with
`ACE_ENABLE_SWAP_ON_WRITE` and this build was not — a `TAO_OutputCDR`
constructed big-endian reports `do_byte_swap() == 1` and still writes
`01000000` for a `long` of 1. Over GIOP the byte order is not the
stream's to report: §9.4 carries it in the message header's flag byte, and
a capture on loopback (`tools/wire-capture`, 2026-08-13) has TAO sending
little-endian requests and **JacORB sending big-endian ones** on the same
host. So "LE only" and "BE only" are true of what these two stream
classes can be made to write and are not a claim about what the ORBs
negotiate.
`org.jacorb.orb.CDROutputStream` has no `setLittleEndian`; only
`CDRInputStream` does. The probes refuse the order they cannot write
rather than labelling host-order bytes as the other one.

`docs/corba-column.md` has the harness, the corpus totals and the
verdicts. This section is the bytes.

### CORBA has two wide-character encodings, and the DDS split follows them

§9.3.1.6 gives `wchar` and `wstring` one form under GIOP 1.1 and another
under GIOP 1.2. Both were taken from one ORB, by handing
`TAO_OutputCDR` the GIOP minor version and changing nothing else.

```idl
struct W { octet head; wchar c; octet mid; wstring s; octet tail; };
```

with `head=0x11`, `c=U+0061`, `mid=0x22`, `s="ab"`, `tail=0xAB`,
little endian:

```
TAO giop 1.1   11 be28f3 61000000 22 000000 03000000 61000000 62000000 00000000 ab
TAO giop 1.2   11 04 61000000 22       08000000 61000000 62000000          ab
```

`be28f3` is the probe's buffer at TAO's alignment padding, not a value:
`ACE_OutputCDR::adjust` writes nothing there. Over GIOP those three
octets carry the previous request's bytes (`tools/wire-capture`), so they
are not TAO's either — on any path TAO determines nothing at a fill
position.

| | GIOP 1.1 | GIOP 1.2 |
|---|---|---|
| `wchar` | a fixed-width value in the transmission code set, aligned to its width | a **one-octet length**, then that many octets, aligned to **1** |
| `wstring` | a count of **characters including a terminating NUL** | a count of **octets**, no terminator |

Beside §4's RTI row — `03000000 61000000 62000000 00000000 ab` for
`"ab"` under XCDR1, and `61000000 ab` for the scalar `wchar`:

> **RTI Connext's XCDR1 wide-character encoding is CORBA GIOP 1.1's,
> byte for byte.** The four-byte character, the alignment to four, the
> character count, the terminating NUL. Not a vendor's arbitrary
> reading — the older of the two CORBA forms, which is what an XCDR1
> path that means "CORBA CDR" would implement.

So `WstringLengthPolicy::SPECIFICATION` is GIOP 1.2's `wstring` and
`CharacterCountTerminated` is GIOP 1.1's. Fast DDS's `CharacterCount` —
a count of characters with **no** terminator — is neither: it is GIOP
1.1's length with GIOP 1.2's absence of a terminator, and no edition of
CORBA CDR or of XTypes produces it.

### The `wchar` no DDS implementation writes

All three ORBs write GIOP 1.2's length-prefixed scalar `wchar`. No DDS
implementation does, and XTypes Table 31 is why: it makes Char16 a
fixed-width primitive of size 2 and alignment 2, which is neither CORBA
form.

```idl
@final struct Sample { wchar first; wchar second; };   // U+00E4, U+1234
```

```
zerodds  LE   e4003412
omniorb  LE   02 e400 02 3412          (UTF-16 units)
tao      LE   04 e4000000 04 34120000  (UCS-4 units)
jacorb   BE   02 00e4 02 1234          (UTF-16 units)
```

The split runs along the specification boundary and not along a vendor
one: the ORBs on one side, the DDS stacks on the other. Nothing in `WstringLengthPolicy` reaches the
ORB form, so a topic with a scalar `wchar` cannot be exchanged with any
of the three in either direction — `docs/corba-dialect-followup.md`
item 1.

### omniORB writes a byte-order mark, which §7.4.1.1.2 forbids

```idl
@final struct Sample { wstring w; };   // w = "aä"
```

```
omniorb  LE   06000000 fffe 6100 e400
zerodds  LE   04000000      6100 e400
```

The count is six because U+FEFF's two octets are in it. The OMG code-set
specification allows a BOM for UTF-16 under GIOP 1.2 and lets it decide
the content's byte order; §7.4.1.1.2 says no BOM. No option was passed —
omniORB selects its own default wide code set once `ORB_init` has run,
and without an ORB it takes SIGSEGV in `omniCodeSet` rather than
choosing one.

A reader following §7.4.1.1.2 returns U+FEFF as the first character of a
well-formed string of the right length and has nothing to object to.
Same class as Cyclone's unswapped big-endian content. Item 2 of the
followup.

### `long double`: three ORBs, three answers, no binary128

```idl
struct S { octet head; long double d; octet tail; };   // d = 1.5
```

```
omniorb  11 00000000000000 0000000000000000c0ff3f000000000080 ab   (25)
tao      11 00000000000000 0000000000000000c0ff3f000000000000 ab   (25)
jacorb   11 00000000000000 3ff8000000000000                   ab   (17)
```

- **omniORB and TAO** put `d` at payload offset 8 and give it sixteen
  octets, holding x87 80-bit extended — `…c0` `ff3f` is the significand
  and the biased exponent — followed by six octets of padding. **Neither
  writes those six**: omniORB's come out uninitialised and TAO's come out
  zero, and both are the buffer the probe handed them. Over GIOP both
  carry the previous request's octets (`tools/wire-capture`).
- **JacORB** writes **eight** octets holding an IEEE-754 binary64. The
  IDL-to-Java mapping §1.5.2 has no `long double`, so `jacorb idl`
  declares the member `public double d;`. A peer reading sixteen octets
  gets the next member's bytes.

Neither is §9.3.1.3 Figure 9.2's binary128. Five implementations have
now been asked and none writes it. What the run does settle is the
**layout**: size 16 and alignment 8 under XCDR1, from two foreign
implementations, which is the half `wire-feature-inventory.md` row C7
records as checked against no foreign one.

### A union discriminator that selects no member

```idl
union U2 switch (long) { case 1: long one; };
struct S { octet head; U1 a; U1 b; U1 c; U2 d; U3 e; octet tail; };
```

with `d._d = 42` and no member set, omniORB writes `2a000000` and
nothing else. `wire-feature-inventory.md` row J3 — "a discriminator
value that selects no member writes no member" — records **none** in
column 3; it has one now.

The same run settles two more of the union rules, in the same 45 bytes
(`11 7b790f 01000000 07000000 03000000 0000000000 00f83f 63000000 0900 0000 2a000000 00000000 05000000 ab`):

- a case with two labels takes the discriminator the sample set, not the
  first label — `_d = 3` for `case 2: case 3:`;
- a `default:` branch reached by a value of its own keeps that value —
  `_d = 99` with the default member written after it.

`7b790f` is omniORB's uninitialised padding after `head`.

### omniORB does not clear alignment padding

Sixteen of omniORB's corpus differences are this and nothing else:

```
sequence-struct-final LE
zerodds   … 01000000 02000000 ffffffff …
omniorb   … 01000000 0200ddb3 ffffffff …
```

`ddb3` differs between two runs of the same case. §7.4.3.2 leaves
ALIGN's padding content unspecified and this project writes zero, which
is row A4's reading; omniORB is the second implementation family whose
serialiser writes nothing there, after RTI in §2. None of the sixteen is
in the **trailing** padding §7.4.1.1 does fix.

**"Only a difference in what a reader ignores" is now measured rather
than assumed, and it holds for omniORB and not for the reason given.**
`tools/wire-capture`, 2026-08-13, over IIOP: omniORB's fill octets on the
wire are the previous request's, so they are not this uninitialised stack
either — they are deterministic within a connection and still not a
function of the sample. A reader ignores them in both cases. What does
*not* hold is the parallel to RTI: RTI's RTPS layer writes zero at every
fill position, so RTI's `0800` in §2 was the probe's buffer and RTI is
not in this family at all.

### The read direction, where an ORB is handed this project's bytes

The same 218 cases, both orders, `--in` instead of `--values`. The
comparison is the canonical JSON, so a difference here is a difference
in values. omniORB reads 374 of 432 back identically, TAO 344 and
JacORB 336; every difference is a wide character or JacORB's `default:`
branch, and there is no third kind.

**Both ORBs decode a `wstring`'s code units as UTF-16 big-endian
whatever the stream's byte order is.** The length word they read in the
stream's order — every count and every element length comes out right —
and the content they do not.

```idl
@final struct Sample { wstring items[3]; long tail; };   // "", "äZ", "ሴ"
```

```
little-endian stream          big-endian stream
zerodds  "", "äZ", "ሴ"        "", "äZ", "ሴ"
omniorb  "", U+E400 U+5A00,   "", U+00E4 U+005A,
             U+3412                U+1234
jacorb   the same as omniORB   the same as omniORB
```

§7.4.1.1.2 makes the units the stream's, through `ESWAP` per code unit
(row A10); the OMG code-set rule for GIOP 1.2 makes them UTF-16's own,
big-endian in the absence of a byte-order mark. Each side is
self-consistent — omniORB writes a BOM *so that* its reader knows which
to use, and this project writes none because the clause forbids one —
and on a little-endian wire they cannot talk. It is the same
undecidability as Cyclone's unswapped content in §4, arriving from the
other direction.

**omniORB refuses a bare `wchar`, loudly.** `primitive-wchar` under
XCDR1 LE is `e4003412` from this project; omniORB reads the first octet
as GIOP 1.2's length, gets 0xE4 = 228, runs off the end and raises
`CORBA::MARSHAL`. 32 runs over eight cases. That is the read-direction
proof of the `wchar` finding and it is the *good* failure mode.

**JacORB loses a discriminator that selects no member.**
`union-default-unselected` with `_d = 99` comes back `{"_d":0}` from
JacORB and `{"_d":99}` from omniORB, from TAO and from this project —
the read half of the `default:` limitation above.

**Nothing about narrow strings.** `"grüße → 世界"` and `"été"` come back
from all three exactly as written, in both byte orders. Worth checking,
because CORBA gives a `string` a transmission code set — ISO-8859-1 by
default — where §7.4.1.1.2 makes it UTF-8 unconditionally, and an ORB
that translated would return `?` for every character outside Latin-1.
None does.

### What the ORB front ends refuse

Each refusal is the front end's own words.

| construct | omniORB | TAO | JacORB |
|---|---|---|---|
| `union switch (octet\|int8\|uint8\|wchar)` | `Syntax error in union declaration` | `union with illegal discriminator type` | `Syntax error` |
| `fixed<P,S>` | takes it | `fixed data types are not supported` | takes it |
| `union switch (unsigned long\|long long\|unsigned long long)` | takes it | takes it | `Illegal case label <3735928559> for integral switch type int` |
| `struct D : B` | `Syntax error in struct definition` | `Missing '{' or illegal syntax following struct identifier` | `Syntax error` |
| `int8`, `uint8` | `'int8' not found` | `error in lookup of symbol: int8` | `Undefined name: int8` |

CORBA IDL's `switch_type_spec` is an integer type, a char type, a
boolean type, an enumeration or a scoped name; `octet` is none of them.
This project's front end accepts all four — `union-discriminator-octet`
and the three beside it are corpus cases with recorded bytes — which
makes it looser than CORBA IDL and than IDL 4.2. Item 3 of the followup.

JacORB has one limitation that is not a rule and costs six cases: for a
`default:` branch it generates

```java
public void fraction (int _discriminator, double _x) {
    if (_discriminator != 0) throw new org.omg.CORBA.BAD_OPERATION();
```

hard-coding the one discriminator value it picked and rejecting every
other, so a union whose discriminator falls in the default range and is
not zero can be neither built nor read. omniORB takes `_d = 9` and
produces this project's bytes exactly:

```
union-with-default, _d = 9, fraction = π
omniorb  0900000000000000182d4454fb210940ffffffff
zerodds  0900000000000000182d4454fb210940ffffffff
```


## Reproducing

The byte gate, from a checkout, for every row it covers:

```
tools/byte-gate/gate.sh --cases point
tools/byte-gate/gate.sh --out regenerated.tsv          # all 51 cases
tools/wire-oracle/gate.sh --out regenerated-oracle.tsv # the other 17
tools/byte-gate/verify.sh                              # regenerate and compare
```

Twelve minutes on the Linux test host for all four vendors, both byte
orders, both encoding versions. A vendor that is not installed is named
with the number of rows it did not produce and the run continues.

Both byte orders come out of one driver. Cyclone and Fast DDS each have
a big-endian entry point of their own — `dds_stream_write_sampleBE` and
`Cdr::BIG_ENDIANNESS` — and the template takes the choice as a
substitution. RTI does not: `serialize_to_cdr_buffer_ex` is native by
definition, so its big-endian rows go through the body of
`tools/wireprobe/rti-template.c`, which is the wrapper's own code with
the low bit of the encapsulation id cleared. That template is shared
with `wireprobe-rti` rather than copied, so the two cannot drift.

The earlier arrangement — `/root/byte-gate/gate/gate.sh` for little
endian and `/root/byte-gate/gate-be/run.sh` for big, on one machine —
is what this replaces.

The probes, for any case and either byte order. One command line, three
programs:

```
export WIREPROBE_FILL=<target>/wireprobe-fill
for probe in cyclone rti fastdds; do
    tools/wireprobe/wireprobe-$probe --idl point.idl --type Point \
        --values point.json --encoding xcdr2 --endian be
done
```

The three implementations of the last section have their own case set,
[`tools/wire-oracle/`](../../../../tools/wire-oracle/). It is a second
case directory behind the same driver, so a case added for one of them
cannot disturb a run of the first three.

```
tools/wire-oracle/gate.sh --cases mut_lengthcodes
tools/wire-oracle/gate.sh --cases map_val_struct --vendors opendds
```

OpenDDS takes a `fill.odds.inc` of its own beside the others, because
its C++ mapping assigns to members where Fast DDS's calls setters; a
case without one is recorded as `unfilled` and not attempted. It runs
`tao_idl -Sa -St --idl-version 4` for the types and `opendds_idl` for
the `TypeSupport`, then `OpenDDS::DCPS::Serializer` over
`Encoding::KIND_XCDR1` and `KIND_XCDR2` in both byte orders — one
binary, four rows.

The two hand-written ORB harnesses, `tools/wire-oracle/omni/` and
`tools/wire-oracle/jacorb/`, are what asked each ORB about
`fixed<P,S>`: `omniidl -bcxx` and a `cdrMemoryStream`,
`org.jacorb.idl.parser` and a `CDROutputStream`, one whole struct
through the generated marshaller and no case directory.
`tools/wire-oracle/fixed-orbs.sh` builds and runs both.

The CORBA **column** is not those. It is three probes on the same
command line as the other four, under `tools/wireprobe/`, and it takes
any corpus case:

```
d=tests/interop-corpus/union-with-default
tools/wireprobe/wireprobe-omniorb --idl $d/type.idl --type "$(cat $d/type)" \
    --values $d/values.json --encoding xcdr1 --endian le

tools/corba-oracle/corba-sweep.sh sweep.tsv   # 218 cases, both orders
tools/corba-oracle/corba-read.sh  read.tsv    # the same, read back
```

The three ORBs are not in the `ci-interop` image, so these rows are the
test host's and stay there. The harness does not.

`--encoding` takes the XCDR1 forms only: XCDR2 is XTypes §7.4.2 and
`pl-cdr1` is rule (23), neither of which an ORB has. `--emit` takes
`payload` only, because CORBA CDR has no encapsulation for a top-level
parameter — GIOP §9.4 carries the byte order in the message header.

The measurements above that no corpus case can carry — `long double`,
the two GIOP wide forms, the union rules — are one file each under
[`tools/corba-oracle/targeted/`](../../../../tools/corba-oracle/targeted/).
They are outside the corpus because each needs a construct that would
make every member after it unreadable.

The Rust programs the probes call — `wireprobe-zerodds`,
`wireprobe-fill`, `wireprobe-dump`, `wireprobe-corba-idl` — are
`cargo build -p zerodds-wire-probe --bins` in this checkout. That is
`wire-probe`'s dependency closure and nothing else, nine crates, sixteen
seconds cold on the test host, which is why the sweeps take
`WIREPROBE_TARGET` and not a deployed copy.
